analysis.one_liner: Lets loans keep their original interest rates when sold to other companies, even above state rate caps.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 245-171 on February 14, 2018, but the Senate Banking Committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes into federal law the "valid when made" rule: if a loan's interest rate was legal when a bank made it, the rate stays legal even after the loan is sold to another company, and state laws that cap interest rates cannot block the new owner from collecting. Supporters say this keeps a market for buying and selling loans running, which keeps credit flowing. Opponents say it lets nonbank lenders partner with banks to charge rates that states have outlawed, and then sell those loans so the high rates follow the borrower forever.
analysis.who_benefits: Nonbank lenders, fintech companies, and debt buyers gain the most: they can originate loans through partner banks at rates states would forbid, sell the loans, and enforce the original high rate no matter what state law says. Banks gain a more valuable loan-origination-for-sale business. Borrowers get continued access to credit that might otherwise be pulled back, though often at higher rates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nonbank lenders, fintech firms, and banks

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that a bank loan valid when made as to its maximum interest rate "shall remain valid with respect to such rate regardless of whether the loan is subsequently sold, assigned, or otherwise transferred to a third party," and that the buyer may enforce it "notwithstanding any State law to the contrary." [S5]

The bill's findings argue that legal certainty about transferred loans widens the pool of loan buyers and lowers the cost of credit at origination, and that a court decision (Madden v. Midland) disagreeing with this rule had disproportionately cut off credit to low- and moderate-income borrowers with lower credit scores. [S5]
Supporters framed the bill as protecting consumers' access to credit after a federal appeals court ruling created doubt about whether loan buyers could enforce original loan terms. [S5]

analysis.who_pays: Borrowers in states with interest-rate caps bear the cost: a loan originated by a partner bank can carry a rate those states banned, and the rate follows the loan to whoever buys it. State governments lose the power to enforce their own usury laws against these loans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Borrowers in states with rate caps

drawbacks.text: The bill's own text says a transferred loan's rate may be enforced "notwithstanding any State law to the contrary," which overrides state interest-rate caps for any loan that touches a bank at origination. [S5]

In practice, this opens the door to "rent-a-bank" arrangements: a nonbank lender that could not legally charge a state's cap itself can originate the loan through a partner bank and then buy the loan, keeping the higher rate alive. Consumer advocates warned this would revive high-cost lending in states that had banned it; the bill's supporters dispute that framing and argue the alternative is less credit, not cheaper credit. [S5]

The bill does not add any new rate cap of its own; for loans made by national banks, federal law already allows rates up to what the bank's home state permits, so the practical effect is to extend that freedom to the secondary market rather than to lower any borrower's rate. [S5]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real case for the bill: a court ruling had cast doubt on loan sales, and legal uncertainty can dry up credit for subprime borrowers. But the bill goes beyond fixing that uncertainty. It affirmatively blocks states from applying their own rate caps to transferred loans, which is exactly the tool nonbank high-cost lenders need to reach states that banned those rates. Borrowers who keep access to credit benefit; borrowers who end up paying rates their state legislature voted to outlaw pay for it.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in February 2018, but the Senate sent it to its Banking Committee the next day and no vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 42-17 on November 15, 2017, and reported it on January 30, 2018. [S7]
The House Rules Committee set up floor consideration under a closed rule, meaning no amendments were allowed, and the House passed the bill 245-171 on February 14, 2018. [S7]
The vote split heavily by party: 229 of 237 House Republicans voted yes, while 170 of 193 House Democrats voted no. [S8]
The Senate received the bill on February 15, 2018, referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, and took no further action for the rest of the Congress. [S7]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, state interest-rate caps stayed in place as a check on bank-partnership lending, and nonbank and fintech lenders did not get the federal guarantee that buyers of their loans can enforce rates states have banned. Borrowers in rate-cap states are no worse off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State rate caps and the consumers behind them

for.name: Rep. Patrick McHenry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in July 2017 and shepherded it through committee to House passage.

for.name: Rep. Jeb Hensarling
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill through his committee, which approved it 42-17, and demanded the recorded vote on passage.

for.name: Online and marketplace lending industry
for.role: Fintech and nonbank lenders whose business model depends on selling originated loans
for.what_they_did: Backed federal valid-when-made legislation to overturn the legal uncertainty created by the Madden v. Midland ruling.

against.name: 170 of 193 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, arguing the bill would override state consumer-protection rate caps.

against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee

against.name: Consumer and civil justice groups
against.role: Organizations protecting borrowers and state usury laws
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as a giveaway that would let high-cost lenders dodge state interest-rate caps through bank partnerships.

sides.party_line_note: House passage was 245-171 with Republicans nearly unanimous (229-1) and Democrats opposed (16-170).

industries.industry: Nonbank consumer, installment, and fintech lenders
industries.note: These lenders cannot export interest rates on their own, but through partner banks they could originate loans at rates a state forbids, sell them, and enforce the original rate "notwithstanding any State law to the contrary." The bill is the legal foundation that makes high-cost lending through bank partnerships safe for loan buyers. [S5]

The bill makes bank-originated loans more valuable to sell, because every buyer is guaranteed to keep the original rate, and it creates fee income for banks that lend through fintech partners. Banks and their backers argue this liquidity lowers credit costs at origination and keeps credit available to lower-score borrowers. [S5]

The bill arose directly from a dispute over whether a debt buyer could collect a loan's original interest rate; under this bill, a purchaser of charged-off debt can enforce the original rate even if state law would treat it as usurious. [S5]

industries.industry: State governments and their usury laws
industries.note: States lose the ability to cap what borrowers pay on any loan that originated at a bank and was later sold, which is the main tool states use to protect residents from high-cost credit. [S5]
